AuthorizeResponse.title: AuthorizeResponse

ClaimBatchResponse.description:
``POST /scrape/claims/claim-batch``.

``listings`` is built from the claim statement's own column list, so its
element shape belongs to that SQL rather than to this file and stays
free-form.
ClaimBatchResponse.title: ClaimBatchResponse

CompletedResponse.description: ``POST /coordination/complete`` -- the phase it landed in, and which generation.
CompletedResponse.title: CompletedResponse

CoordinationState.description:
``GET /coordination/status`` -- the authoritative record.

The operator-facing view, wider than the metrics query beside it: every
phase timestamp and the request's own narrative. Timestamps are ISO strings
rather than datetimes because ``_iso`` has already converted them.
CoordinationState.title: CoordinationState

DrainStatusResponse.description:
``GET /coordination/drain-status`` -- fail-closed drain aggregation.

``sources`` carries one entry per evidence source, each of which reports
``known`` or ``unknown`` rather than guessing a zero -- an unreadable
source blocks the deploy, which is the whole design.
DrainStatusResponse.title: DrainStatusResponse

HealthResponse.description: ``GET /health`` everywhere: process liveness, never dependency health.
HealthResponse.title: HealthResponse

HostEvidenceResponse.description:
``POST /coordination/host-evidence`` -- the receipt for a submission.

``gates`` and ``evidence_digests`` are echoed from the request so the
caller can see exactly what was stored under ``evidence_id``.
HostEvidenceResponse.title: HostEvidenceResponse

IntentStatusResponse.description:
``GET /deploy/status``.

``number_running`` and ``min_started_at`` come from the joined in-flight
count and are absent from the no-row and read-failed shapes, which is why
they are optional and the other four are not. ``pause_long_jobs`` is the
column default when there is no intent -- shape, not a claim about a
deploy, as ``_no_intent`` says.
IntentStatusResponse.title: IntentStatusResponse

LocalDrainResponse.description:
``GET /coordination/local-drain`` -- this process's own job evidence.

``ops`` cannot ask itself over HTTP for the reason every other service is
asked that way, so it reports ``job_snapshot()`` directly and labels the
source. ``known`` is always ``True`` here: an in-process count cannot be
unavailable the way a service across the network can.
LocalDrainResponse.title: LocalDrainResponse

PhaseResponse.description:
The phase transitions that answer with the phase they reached.

``/coordination/begin-drain``, ``/coordination/cancel`` and
``/coordination/begin-validation``.
PhaseResponse.title: PhaseResponse

ReleaseClaimsResponse.description:
``POST /scrape/claims/release`` -- and there is no ``status`` key.

Stated plainly because a caller has been reading one for months.
``airflow/dags/scrape_detail_pages.py`` logs ``result.get("status")`` from
this endpoint and has logged ``status=None`` every run since the DAG was
written. The repair is not to add the field -- it is this model, which
makes the absence checkable instead of leaving it to be discovered.
ReleaseClaimsResponse.title: ReleaseClaimsResponse

RotationResponse.description:
``POST /scrape/rotation/advance`` -- three exits, one shape.

A slot that is due answers ``slot``, ``run_id`` and ``configs``; a request
that arrived too soon answers ``reason`` and ``last_run_minutes_ago``
alongside empty versions of the first three; an empty queue answers the
first three with nothing in them. The two refusal fields are optional
because only one exit sets them, and declaring them here is what makes
"why did I get no configs" answerable from the contract.
RotationResponse.title: RotationResponse

post.description:
Releases the intent lock on the DB.

A failure here is the quiet one. ``redeploy.sh`` calls this from its exit
trap, so a deploy that succeeded and then failed to release still exits 0
and sends no alert, leaving every gated DAG parked. Whatever this returns is
the operator's only account of that, which is why it is no longer one word.

post.description:
Atomically claims the next batch of listings from the detail scrape queue.

Creates a run row, inserts claims into detail_scrape_claims using
ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE so stale claims are re-claimed cleanly.

Returns {run_id, listings: [{listing_id, vin, canonical_detail_url, ...}]}.
Returns {run_id, listings: []} if the queue is empty.

Releases claims after a scrape batch completes.

Deletes the claim rows for the given run_id and records, on the same
transaction, that a detail request was spent on each listing the scraper
actually attempted.

That second write is the loop guard (Plan 147). Before it, the only thing
stopping a listing being re-fetched was a timestamp written by the
*processing* service two hops downstream, so any break in that chain —
processing paused, crashed, backed up, or a parser gap — left the claims
deleted, the guard unwritten, and the same batch re-claimed fifteen minutes
later. The component that spends the resource now records having spent it.

last_detail_fetched_at is set for 'ok' and 'failed' results but not
'skipped': the column means "we spent a request", and a failed fetch spent
one. Blocked and delisted listings keep their existing cooldown paths; this
does not replace them.

Note that the three-way rule is a contract no caller exercises today.
scrape_detail_pages reports 'ok' for every claimed listing regardless of
outcome, which is correct for a loop guard — the batch consumed requests
either way — so in production every released listing is stamped.

The DELETE is this handler's only other statement. It does not mark any run
finished and never has, despite what its docstring claimed until Plan 147:
there is no runs-table write here.

Atomically claims the next rotation slot due for scraping.

Two guards:
1. min_idle_minutes (default 1439 = 23h59m): each slot must wait this long
   before it can fire again.
2. min_gap_minutes (default 230 = ~3h50m): blocks if ANY config's
   last_queued_at falls within this window. Prevents multiple slots from
   firing in rapid succession even if all have stale timestamps.

Returns {"slot": null, "configs": [], "run_id": null} when nothing is due.
Returns {"slot": ..., "configs": [...], "run_id": "<uuid>"} when work is claimed.
run_id is a fresh UUID for the caller to pass to the scraper; no runs row is inserted.
